record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted figure content is garbled, but the main text and relevant tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies LLM-generated neuron explanations and activation simulation to GPT-2 and CRATE, reporting automated interpretation scores. This bears conceptually on whether explanations predict neuron activations, but it does not measure the Qwen3 neuron-pole shares.
record.gate_note: Relevant results are the automated interpretation scores in Table 2. The paper also reports next-token prediction performance, SAE reconstruction and recovery results, and qualitative steering examples; these do not measure the claim versions. Layer-wise scores in Figure 6 and alternate explanation/simulation-model evaluations in Tables 6–7 bear on automated scoring but are not included among the rows below.
record.test_reason: Uses the Bills et al. explain-and-simulate scoring on GPT-2 MLP neurons (and CRATE) and reports the scores. Overall mean correlations are 1.4–14.2%, which bears directly on V7. The random-only versus top-and-random gap bears on V6. The CRATE-versus-GPT-2 contrast is an architecture effect on the same scores, which bears on V4 in language models. Explainer and simulator are Mistral-7B and LLaMA-2-7B, weaker than the original GPT-4 setup.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that CRATE's built-in sparse coding gives higher neuron interpretability than GPT-2, by up to 103% relative, for L∈{2,3,6,12}, and more layer-stable interpretability. They attribute this to more consistent and specific activations, and show the gain is not explained by worse performance or fewer parameters. They acknowledge CRATE's next-token prediction is worse than GPT-2's. The record omits that CRATE does not beat GPT-2 at L=1.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LLM-generated explanations and simulated activations with established OpenAI and Anthropic interpretation metrics, rather than auditing named neuron poles or estimating the share of neurons with a specified number of jobs. The paper uses Mistral-7B-instruct and LLaMA-2-7B for accessible evaluations and compares CRATE with GPT-2.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretation scores vary by metric, model depth, and model; Appendix B also evaluates alternative explanation and simulation model sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: CRATE's interpretation scores vary much less across layers than GPT-2's (Table 2 variance, e.g. L=12 Anthropic 18.3 vs 24.65; L=6 2.01 vs 32.56).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Built-in sparse coding makes neuron interpretability more uniform across layers.

record.peer_reviewed: Second Conference on Parsimony and Learning (CPAL 2025), Oral
record.problems: The reported interpretation scores are means across layers, not the fraction of neurons above a stated good-score threshold. No such threshold is defined. The study evaluates GPT-2-sized models rather than modern large models, and reports that CRATE has worse next-token prediction performance than GPT-2.
record.rows_left_out: The row cap was not reached. Layer-wise scores in Figure 6, alternative explainer comparisons in Table 6, alternative simulator comparisons in Table 7, checkpoint results in Table 4, and SAE comparisons were not extracted because they do not directly report the fraction of neurons with good explanation scores.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no neuron-pole job shares.
Only tiny GPT-2-sized dense models are tested; no MoE or large models, and no shares.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron reanalysis.
No vision models and no 5%→99% estimates. Tool improvements are only via SAEs, not better neuron-reading tools on raw neurons.
No per-neuron good-score threshold or fraction is reported in the main text; only means are given, plus a histogram in Fig. 12.

missing.what: Per-neuron histograms of interpretation scores for CRATE-12L and GPT2-12L, needed for the share of neurons with good scores.
GPT-3.5-turbo vs Mistral-7B explainer scores per layer (similar values).
LLaMA-2-7B vs 70B simulator scores (70B generally higher, still low).
Post-hoc SAE effects on scores: GPT2-SAE +38.1 Anthropic and +6.5 TaR; CRATE-SAE −10.2 TaR and +34.8 Anthropic; SAE matches GPT-2 on OpenAI metrics. This is a tool effect on the interpretable share.
Layer-wise scores showing CRATE above GPT-2 on almost all layers.

record.verdict_notes: Bills et al. is an original source of the phenomenon, but this study is not, so verdicts are allowed. CRATE rows are the study's own architecture. They are kept because they are the V4 architecture test, and their low absolute scores also bear on V7. Each row carries one state, which is given for its first listed version; the problem text gives the states for the other versions. All scores are layer-averaged correlations in %, with the last layer excluded.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B, count neuron poles by number of jobs, or report the claimed percentages.
The study tests GPT-2-sized models, not similar modern models, mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters; it does not measure the claimed shares.
The study does not investigate InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.

The study compares a white-box architecture with GPT-2 using interpretation scores, but does not test the essay's claims about InceptionV1-sized vision models, architecture or tool effects on the claimed share, or the estimates from about 5% to about 99%.
The study does not test whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behaviour without a trained replacement model and reconstruction error.
The study reports random-only simulation scores, but does not report a separate count of explanations that fit activating examples and then fail on a held-out activation dataset.

The study reports mean automated interpretation scores, not the fraction of individual neurons above a stated good-score threshold. Alternate explanation and simulation model results are reported in Appendix B.
